summary:
Iceland ranks first of 121 jurisdictions surveyed by Equaldex as a good place for gay and lesbian people, at 93 per cent. The same source records that same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women, same-sex marriage is recognised, gender change carries no restrictions, non-binary identity is recognised, discrimination is illegal with hate-crime protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity, bathroom access is protected, conversion therapy is banned, and intersex infant surgery is fully banned.

Legal gender recognition operates on a self-determination basis under the 2019 reform, which took effect on 1 January 2020 and was implemented in January 2021. Minors may change their legal gender with parental consent, an X third-gender marker is available, and medical interventions on intersex children are prohibited except where health-related. The statute replaced an earlier law that was already regarded as among the most progressive in Europe, and activists including the chair of Trans Ísland continue to map the practical difficulties that remain.

Discrimination protection rests on the 1996 Penal Code amendments, which made it an offence to publicly attack a person or group through mockery, defamation, abuse or threats because of their sexual orientation, and on a 2014 amendment that added gender identity as a prohibited ground. Discrimination in education has been unlawful since 2008. The Equality Complaints Committee, operated through Ísland.is, is the official complaints mechanism for equality complaints, and Outright International reports that LGBTI organisations can register while noting acknowledged gaps in protection.

Police-recorded potential hate crimes rose to 16 cases in 2023, three times the previous year, with 11 recorded in 2024 and 7 in the current year. Samtökin 78 has called for stronger hate-crime legislation as recorded incidents climb. The national emergency service, 112.is, describes hate crime as an umbrella term for offences committed from prejudice or hatred, publishes guidance for victims and perpetrators, and sets out reporting routes for abuse against queer people, whom it notes are more likely to be victims of violence.

Relationship recognition has accumulated in stages. Registered partnerships from 1996 already granted same-sex couples many of the rights, responsibilities and benefits of marriage, including the ability to adopt stepchildren; stepchild adoption by a partner was permitted from 2000; and on 27 June 2006 same-sex couples gained equal access to joint adoption of children alongside public IVF insemination treatment. The 2010 same-sex marriage vote passed unanimously, 49 to 0. The conversion therapy ban followed in 2023 on a 53 to 0 vote with 3 abstentions.

GOV.UK travel advice for Iceland states that same-sex sexual activity is legal and same-sex relationships are recognised in law, and sets out dedicated LGBT+ guidance for British visitors.
tangentialFactors:
Section 178 of the Penal Code criminalised same-sex relations between 1869 and 1940, and public antipathy towards LGBT people stayed high until the 1980s, when some of the first Icelanders to come out publicly, Hörður Torfason and Anna Kristjánsdottir, faced discrimination and ridicule. State policy has since reversed through the 1996 anti-discrimination amendments, the 2010 marriage vote and the 2023 conversion therapy ban.

Public expression of support is visible. Reykjavík Pride drew about 100,000 people in 2015, and in 2016 President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson became the first head of state to attend a gay pride parade. A gay scene of bars and cafés exists in Reykjavík, but the sparse population elsewhere means there is almost no scene outside the capital, and Akureyri has no gay bars.

A blood donation restriction on men who have sex with men was challenged by a lawsuit in 2014, relaxed to a four-month deferral in September 2021 and lifted entirely from September 2026.

The age of consent was set at 14 in 1992 and raised to 15 in 2007, applied regardless of gender or sexual orientation. A 2000 Gallup poll found 53 per cent of Icelanders supported lesbian and gay adoption rights against 35 per cent opposed.
localsOnly:
Since 2008 it has been illegal to discriminate against people on the basis of their sexual orientation in education. From 2016 the town of Hafnarfjörður has included information about same-sex relationships in its eighth-grade sex education lessons, covering ages 14 and 15, and the Queer Student Association of Iceland runs social activities and field trips for University of Iceland students.

Blood donation eligibility is a resident-facing health rule: the four-month deferral applied from September 2021 and the restriction was lifted entirely from September 2026.

Outright International records that LGBTI organisations can register in Iceland, and the Equality Complaints Committee is the standing institutional route for equality complaints.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory, a travel information page for trans and non-binary visitors and two international hate-crime monitoring pages for Iceland, returned no usable finding and support none of the claims above.

Outright International states that Iceland's laws are progressive with acknowledged gaps in protection, but does not identify which protections are incomplete. The nature and extent of those gaps remain unresolved in this record.

The current-year hate-crime figure of 7 cases is a partial-year count and is not comparable to the full-year totals for 2023 and 2024.

A substantial share of the historical and statutory detail, including Penal Code section 178, the 1996 and 2014 amendments, the adoption and partnership dates and the vote counts, derives from an encyclopaedic country coverage rather than primary legislation, and has not been independently corroborated here.

Whether Icelandic border and document checks accept a foreign-issued X or non-binary marker, and how such documents are handled at screening, is not addressed by any source in the inventory and remains unresolved.
